alt: Seven small family diagrams: nuclear, extended, single-parent, reconstituted, living apart together, child-free couple and beanpole (many generations, few members each). A note adds Therborn’s point that family systems differ across world regions.
caption: There is no single family form: households take many shapes.

alt: Three cards. Parsons, a functionalist, sees positive functions: primary socialisation and stabilising adult personalities. Engels, a Marxist, sees the family serving capitalism. Oakley, a feminist, sees women positioned unequally around domestic labour and childcare. Below, Smart and Stacey on growing family diversity.
caption: Functionalists see benefits, Marxists see capitalism, feminists see inequality.

alt: Rising life expectancy and falling birth rates produce beanpole families: three generations with few members in each. The middle generation becomes the pivot generation, caring for ageing parents above and children below at the same time.
caption: Longer lives and fewer births leave the middle generation caring both ways.

alt: A cycle of four steps around the self-fulfilling prophecy: a teacher labels a pupil, often on limited evidence; the teacher’s expectations change; the pupil is treated differently; the pupil internalises and acts out the label, which confirms it.
caption: A label shapes expectations and treatment until the pupil lives up, or down, to it.

alt: Top: the official curriculum is the subjects formally taught; the hidden curriculum teaches punctuality, respect for authority and competitiveness through routine. Below, three perspectives: functionalist role allocation, Bourdieu on cultural capital reproducing class inequality, and Freire and Illich on schooling suppressing critical thought.
caption: Schools teach more than subjects; the perspectives disagree about what that does.

alt: Four cards on access to education worldwide: provision (free schooling, class sizes, teachers, buildings); poverty (child work, fees, underfunding); gender and other inequalities (early marriage, disability, rural location, conflict, with women about two-thirds of adults lacking basic literacy); and digital access, exposed during COVID-19 closures.
caption: Provision, poverty, gender and digital access all shape who gets an education.

alt: Five methods with what each is strong on and a strength and weakness: questionnaires and structured interviews are reliable; unstructured interviews and participant observation give valid detail; official statistics give large-scale, comparable data but were collected for other purposes. Below, the three tests: reliability, validity and representativeness.
caption: Reliable methods tend to lack depth; valid, detailed methods are hard to repeat.

alt: For a study of bullying in a school, a questionnaire is anonymous and reliable but shallow; unstructured interviews give rich detail but pupils may not open up and the sample is small. The best answer combines them: a questionnaire to measure how widespread bullying is, then interviews with volunteers to understand why.
caption: Recommending a justified combination scores higher than defending one method.
